summary: Is the reference document for the Routing Policy Specification Language, which lets network operators write down routing policies, for example at the AS level. The policies can be detailed enough to generate router configurations, and the language can be extended. It was replaced by RFC 2622.

eli5.summary: It is a language for writing down the rules about whose traffic a network accepts and passes along. Tools can use it to set up routers.

questions: how to write import export policies
subtitle: A language for describing routing policies in a machine-readable format.

tldr.problem: Network operators need to describe complex routing policies: which routes they accept, how they export routes to peers, how they set BGP attributes. These policies are currently described in prose, making them ambiguous and hard for tools to parse or verify.
tldr.mechanism: RPSL is a language and object model for specifying routing policies at the autonomous system (AS) level. It defines classes like aut-num for AS policies, route for origin announcements, and route-set and as-set for grouping routes and ASes. Operators write policy rules that specify import and export actions and filters.
tldr.outcome: Policies can be stored in a distributed database (the Internet Routing Registry), versioned, and used to generate router configurations or to audit routing security. RFC 2280 was replaced by RFC 2622 with similar concepts and additional features.

today: RFC 2280 is a Proposed Standard that was replaced by RFC 2622, which carries forward RPSL with clarifications and enhancements. RPSL remains the standard language for routing policy specification in production routing registries.

sections.title: Routing Policy Language
sections.content:
The Internet routes packets across multiple autonomous systems (ASes). At the boundaries between ASes, operators must decide which routes to import (accept from neighbors), which to export (send to neighbors), and how to set BGP route attributes to influence traffic engineering. Traditionally, these policies are described in prose, making them prone to ambiguity and difficult for tools to understand.

The Routing Policy Specification Language (RPSL) provides a formal notation for expressing these policies. It is object-oriented: policies are stored as structured objects (like route objects, AS policy objects) in a distributed database called the Internet Routing Registry (IRR). This allows policies to be versioned, audited, and used to generate router configurations automatically.
sections.eli5: RPSL is a formal way to write down the rules about which traffic a network sends and accepts. A computer can read RPSL rules and set up routers without human error.

sections.title: Objects and Classes
sections.content:
RPSL is organized around object classes, each representing a piece of routing information. The aut-num class describes an autonomous system and its routing policies (import, export, and default routes). The route class specifies which AS originates a particular IP prefix. The route-set and as-set classes group routes and ASes under a name for reuse in policies.

Supporting classes describe administrative details: the mntner class defines entities authorized to create and modify objects, and the person and role classes provide contact information. The inet-rtr class describes routers and their peers. An import attribute in an aut-num object specifies which routes are accepted from which peers and what actions (modifications to BGP attributes) are applied. An export attribute specifies which routes are sent to which peers. Routes, ASes, and their sets can be defined explicitly by name or implicitly by maintainer.
sections.eli5: RPSL has different types of objects: some describe who controls data, some describe which network owns a route, some list routes or AS numbers, and some write the actual import/export rules.

sections.title: Policy Specification
sections.content:
A policy is expressed via import, export, and default attributes in an aut-num object. Each policy attribute specifies a peering, optional actions, and a filter. For example:

import: from AS2 action pref = 100; accept { 128.9.0.0/16 }

This states: import the prefix 128.9.0.0/16 from AS2 and set its preference to 100. The peering can be as simple as an AS number or as detailed as specific router IP addresses. Actions modify BGP attributes: setting preference values, adding BGP communities, or adjusting the MULTI-EXIT-DISCRIMINATOR. Filters specify which routes match: by address prefix, by AS path (using regular expressions), by route set membership, or by combinations with AND/OR/NOT.
sections.eli5: A policy says: 'For traffic from neighbor AS2, accept these prefixes, change these attributes, and pass it along.' It's like a rule: 'if traffic has these properties, do these things.'

sections.title: Filters and AS-Path Expressions
sections.content:
RPSL filters determine which routes a policy affects. The simplest filter is ANY, which matches all routes. Address prefix filters list specific prefixes or routes sets (groups of prefixes). For example:

accept { 128.9.0.0/16, 128.8.0.0/16 }

Filters can also use AS-path regular expressions to match routes based on which ASes the route traversed. For example, <AS1 AS2 AS3> matches routes that came through AS1, then AS2, then AS3 in that order. Complex patterns like <AS1 .* AS3> (AS1 followed by any sequence of ASes, ending at AS3) are supported using POSIX regex syntax.

Hierarchical set names allow operators to define policy sets at any level: an AS can create a set, and other ASes can create sub-sets under it, providing clear ownership and preventing name collisions.
sections.eli5: A filter says which traffic this policy applies to. It can match by the destination address, by the path the route took, or by grouping rules (like 'all my customer routes').

sections.title: Deployment and Status
sections.content:
RPSL objects are stored in the Internet Routing Registry, a distributed database maintained by regional registries (RIPE, RADB, APNIC, etc.). Network operators register their AS policies, route announcements, and policy templates in the IRR. Tools can then query the IRR to retrieve policies, validate them for consistency, and generate router configurations.

RPSL is extensible: new routing protocols and attributes can be added via the dictionary class. Policy actions and filters are not hardcoded into the language; they are defined in an extensible dictionary. This allows RPSL to accommodate new routing protocols and BGP attributes as they are developed.

RFC 2280 is a Proposed Standard that was replaced by RFC 2622, which refined the language with additional features and clarifications. Both versions define the same core concepts and are used in production routing registries today.
sections.eli5: Network operators around the world store their policies in a shared database so they can be checked and used to configure routers. As routing evolves, the language can be extended to handle new features.

right.desc: Select local routes, apply actions, send to peer.
